title: Fix install upgrade path and republish a working launcher

history.detail:
FAIL: FAIL — Round 1. Audited commit 10b2f0a against the current sprint 2 file, re-read fresh. Working tree clean apart from the known out-of-scope .vscode/settings.json.

What's right: the taxonomy is explicit data, not scattered conditionals (Req 1). .claude/agents and CLAUDE.md are correctly user-owned — I verified by hand that a customised persona survives an upgrade untouched, which is the misclassification the sprint's Risks section says would be most destructive. package.json is 0.1.1 and tag v0.1.1 points at 10b2f0a, i.e. at the code that would actually publish rather than at the earlier bump commit (Req 6). scripts/verify-tarball.sh is a real, runnable procedure and I ran it end-to-end: it passes, and I independently confirmed via npm pack that the tarball now carries only the .gitkeep skeleton (Req 7). scripts/launcher/** is byte-identical to sprint 1's closed state, satisfying the regression criterion. 54 tests pass, run by me.

Three defects. Two are in code this sprint wrote.

BLOCKER 1 — backups are re-consumed as stale framework files on every subsequent run, and the chain grows without bound. A backup written by overwriteFrameworkFile()/removeStaleFrameworkFile() lands *inside* a FRAMEWORK_OWNED directory (e.g. scripts/launcher/run-role.js.bak-0.1.0). On the next run, syncFrameworkPath() collects it in destFilesBefore, doesn't find it in sourceSet, and routes it to removeStaleFrameworkFile(). Reproduced with three real upgrade runs against a simulated stale install:
  run 1 -> run-role.js.bak-0.1.0, state.js.bak-0.1.0
  run 2 -> run-role.js.bak-0.1.0.bak-0.1.1, state.js.bak-0.1.0.bak-0.1.1
  run 3 -> run-role.js.bak-0.1.0.bak-0.1.1.bak-0.1.1
Consequences, in order of how much they matter:
  - Req 2 says overwriting must always be recoverable. After three runs the user's original run-role.js is at run-role.js.bak-0.1.0.bak-0.1.1.bak-0.1.1. That is recoverable only in the sense that the bytes still exist somewhere; nobody will find it.
  - Idempotency is gone. install.js's own summary invites a re-run ("re-run this script if useful"), and a plain re-run with nothing to upgrade now mutates the tree every time. The existing "re-running against its own output is a no-op" test does not catch this because a first install creates no backups — the test and the bug don't intersect.
  - The Removed section reports the installer's own backups as "no longer part of the framework", which is a false statement printed to the user about files the installer itself just wrote.
  - Filenames grow by ~11 bytes per run. Somewhere around 20-25 upgrades this exceeds the 255-byte filename limit and copyFileSync throws ENAMETOOLONG, so the installer eventually fails outright rather than degrading.
Note that LiveQA's Part A upgrade check runs the installer once and would pass. This only appears on the second run.

BLOCKER 2 — a local install copies this repo's live sprint data into the target project. docs/sprints is classified USER_OWNED, which means "copy from source when absent". Running `node /path/to/fully-completely/scripts/install.js` from an empty project — the invocation install.js's own header documents — produced, in my throwaway target:
  docs/sprints/registry.json (this repo's, listing sprints 1 and 2, next_id 3)
  docs/sprints/state/sprint-1.json and sprint-2.json (containing my full QA1 audit text and the maintainer's email address)
  docs/sprints/3-done/sprint-1_...md and 2-in-progress/sprint-2_...md
  docs/sprints/.locks/*.lock (transient lock files, gitignored, copied anyway because collectPaths walks the real filesystem)
This is not only an information leak. The target project now starts life with a registry claiming two sprints exist that have nothing to do with it, so /sprint-new hands out 3 and /sprint-status 1 reports another project's history — the target's sprint state is corrupt from the first command.

To be fair about provenance: docs/sprints was already in the old COPY_PATHS, so the behaviour predates this sprint and is not a regression introduced here. But Req 1 is precisely "classify every installed path", this sprint is the one that made the call, and the comment written above USER_OWNED asserts that "this repo's copy of docs/sprints/ only ever supplies the initial empty-folder skeleton on a genuine first install". That is false for the local-install path, and a comment that states a safety property the code doesn't have is worse than no comment. The .npmignore fix is correct and I confirmed it works, but it fixes the packaging layer while the classification defect it compensates for stays in place — so exactly one of the two documented install paths is safe. USER_OWNED is the wrong category: the correct behaviour is to seed only the phase-folder skeleton and never copy source sprint content at all, in either path.

Answering the direct question on scoping: yes, treating the tarball leak as part of Req 7 was the right call — Req 7 is "verify the tarball before publishing", and discovering the tarball is wrong is the entire point of verifying it. Escalating would have been process for its own sake. The judgement was right; the fix was just applied one layer too far downstream.

FINDING 3 — a symlinked directory inside a framework-owned tree routes deletion outside the framework-owned set. Req 4's acceptance criterion asks me to confirm no input can do this, so I tested it rather than reading it. collectPaths() uses fs.statSync, which follows symlinks, so a symlink at scripts/launcher/linked pointing to ../../my-precious is walked into, and its contents are collected as scripts/launcher/linked/* and treated as stale. Result, reproduced:
  scripts/launcher/linked/notes.txt (no longer part of the framework, backed up ..., then removed)
and the user's my-precious/notes.txt — plainly outside the framework-owned set — was deleted, leaving only notes.txt.bak-0.1.0 in their own directory. Content survives via the backup, so this is not silent data loss, but Req 4 says "Never delete anything outside the framework-owned set" without qualification, and this is a route to exactly that. The fix is small: use fs.lstatSync in collectPaths and refuse to descend into or collect symlinks. Contrived setup, real violation, cheap fix — I'd rather it be closed than argued about.

MINOR — removeDeadGitignoreLines() rewrites the whole .gitignore as raw.split(/\r?\n/).join('\n'), silently converting a CRLF file to LF whenever a dead line is found. Harmless on macOS, but Part B is Windows and this sprint's whole point is that Windows is where the unverified things break. Preserve the file's existing line ending.

On the classification question for the paths the sprint file didn't name: I agree with all of them. scripts/smoke_test.sh, dev2_worktree.sh, worktree_test.sh, install.js and docs/HUMAN_OVERRIDE.md are shipped and maintained upstream and are not customisation surfaces, which is the actual test — "does the user edit this on purpose", not "does it look like a framework file". install.js overwriting itself mid-run is safe: Node reads the module fully at require time, so the running process is unaffected by the replacement. docs/sprints is the only one you got wrong, and it's wrong in the other direction — see Blocker 2.

Required before re-audit: stop treating installer-written backups as framework files (exclude the backup naming pattern from the stale scan, or keep backups outside the framework tree entirely); make docs/sprints seed the skeleton only, in both install paths, and correct the comment; make collectPaths symlink-safe; preserve .gitignore line endings. Add tests for the second-run case specifically — the current no-op test cannot see it — and for the symlink case. Then re-run /sprint-qa1 2.

Nothing here touches Req 6's publish step, which is Pipeman's and which I do not gate on. But this must not publish in its current state: publishing is irreversible, the audience includes workshop students, and a first upgrade cycle would hand them a corrupted registry.

PASS: PASS — Round 2. Audited commit 5628f95 against the current sprint 2 file, re-read fresh and confirmed unchanged since round 1 (last touched at 10b2f0a, no working-tree diff). Working tree otherwise clean apart from the known out-of-scope .vscode/settings.json.

All three blockers and the minor finding are fixed. I re-ran my own round-1 reproductions against the new code rather than accepting the handoff's account of them — which mattered here, because the handoff text arrived corrupted partway through (the test count, the git-tag note, and the closing line were garbled). None of the conclusions below come from that text.

BLOCKER 1 (backup compounding) — FIXED. Backups now carry a distinct .fc-bak- marker and collectPaths() filters any path whose basename contains it, so a backup is never re-collected as stale framework content. Re-ran my exact three-run repro against a simulated stale install:
  run 1: Upgraded 0.1.0 -> 0.1.1, backups run-role.js.fc-bak-0.1.0 and state.js.fc-bak-0.1.0
  run 2: Already at 0.1.1 (re-run, nothing to upgrade), same two backups, no Removed section
  run 3: identical
No nesting, no unbounded filename growth, no false "no longer part of the framework" reports, and idempotency is restored — runs 2 and 3 are genuine no-ops. Req 2's recoverability now means something in practice: the original run-role.js sits at exactly one obvious name, one hop from where it was, and I read its contents back to confirm.

BLOCKER 2 (sprint-data leak) — FIXED, and fixed at the right layer this time. docs/sprints is no longer walked; SPRINT_SKELETON_FILES is an explicit seven-entry allowlist of phase-folder .gitkeep placeholders, special-cased in the USER_OWNED loop. A real local install into an empty directory now produces exactly those seven files and nothing else — no registry.json, zero state/*.json, no sprint markdown, and no .locks/*.lock (which the old directory walk was picking up as a side effect of reading the real filesystem). Confirmed by find over a fresh throwaway target and by grepping it for audit text and the maintainer's email: absent. Both documented install paths are now safe, rather than the packaging layer alone. The comment above USER_OWNED has been rewritten to describe what the code actually enforces and to record why, which is the right correction — the previous version asserted a safety property the code did not have.

BLOCKER 3 (symlink escape) — FIXED. collectPaths() uses lstatSync and returns [] for a symlink rather than descending. Re-ran my exact scenario — a symlinked directory under scripts/launcher/ pointing at an external directory holding a user file — and the external file survives untouched, with no Removed section emitted at all. Req 4's "never delete anything outside the framework-owned set" now holds against the one input I found that could route around it.

MINOR (CRLF) — FIXED for the path Req 4 covers. removeDeadGitignoreLines() detects the file's existing ending and rejoins with it. Verified on a real CRLF .gitignore: the dead line is removed and the surviving lines keep their CRLF endings.

Regression checks, all re-run rather than assumed:
- scripts/launcher/** is byte-identical to sprint 1's closed state across BOTH sprint-2 commits (diffed 78b788d..5628f95), satisfying the regression criterion.
- User-owned protection still holds: a customised agent persona and a customised CLAUDE.md both survive an install untouched and are reported as conflicts. This is the misclassification the sprint's Risks section calls most destructive, so it gets re-checked every round, not just the round it was introduced.
- Tarball still clean: npm pack carries only the seven .gitkeep placeholders, and scripts/verify-tarball.sh runs green end-to-end (exit 0, "TARBALL VERIFICATION PASSED").
- package.json is 0.1.1 and tag v0.1.1 now points at 5628f95, i.e. HEAD, the commit that would actually publish. Re-pointing an unpushed tag is the correct move — a tag marking the earlier commit would have marked code that is no longer what ships, which is precisely the published/source divergence Req 6 exists to make visible. Verified independently via git rev-list, not from the handoff.
- 58 tests, all passing, run by me. The four new ones target the exact gaps I raised: the second-run backup case (which the pre-existing no-op test structurally could not see), the symlink case, a real first install's docs/sprints content, and CRLF preservation.

Two observations, neither blocking and neither requiring action this sprint:

1. The .gitignore ends up with mixed line endings on a CRLF file — removeDeadGitignoreLines() now preserves CRLF, but mergeGitignore()'s append path still joins with a hardcoded \n, so a Windows target finishes with CRLF above and LF in the appended block. Dev Team flagged this as pre-existing and out of scope, and that scoping is right: Req 4 asked only about the dead-line removal, and the sprint's Out of Scope section explicitly protects the merge logic. Git parses a mixed-ending .gitignore without complaint, so this is cosmetic. Worth a follow-up sprint alongside any other merge-logic work, not worth reopening this one.

2. The backup marker changed from .bak- to .fc-bak-, so a backup written by the intermediate 10b2f0a installer would not match the new exclusion and would be churned once into a .fc-bak- name before stabilising. This affects nobody: 10b2f0a was never published (npm still serves 0.1.0) and never shipped to a target. Recording it only so that if anyone did run that intermediate build by hand, the single rename is explained rather than mysterious.

Static gate is clear. This sprint does not close on my verdict: Req 6's publish is Pipeman's operation and I explicitly do not gate on it, and LiveQA owns Part A (first install and upgrade-over-stale against the real installer, including the load-bearing UUID check) and Part B (Windows — the headline `npx fully-completely@0.1.1` then `FC: Start All` check that discharges sprint 1's outstanding Dependencies line, plus backups and state.js removal over paths with spaces and a drive letter). Part A's upgrade check should be run at least twice in a row, not once: a single run passed even before this round's fix, and the second run is where the defect lived.
